report.executiveSummary:
The strongest evidence in this set is legal, and it is the part that should change how the company operates first. California law, not marketing theory, already decides most of what can be promised, published, signed and collected. The down payment on a home improvement contract is capped at $1,000 or ten percent of the price, whichever is less. The contract contents are dictated, including approximate start and finish dates, signed change orders before the covered work starts, and a three day cancellation notice, five days for clients aged 65 and over. The license number has to appear in all advertising, which includes the website. None of that is optional and none of it is a matter of taste.

The second thing worth acting on is that the state's own water ordinance makes a paid design step defensible. On new landscape of 500 square feet or more, or a 2,500 square foot renovation, where a permit or plan check is involved, a documentation package is required, and the design plan may be signed by a licensed landscape contractor rather than a landscape architect. That is a regulated deliverable the company can produce and sign itself. It is the closest thing in this whole body of evidence to a reason a client has to pay for design as its own step. Local cities may set their own thresholds and nobody has checked Redwood City or San Mateo County.

Where the design question is genuinely unsettled is whether a design only agreement, one the client could carry to another builder, is inside what a landscape contractor's license allows, and whether that agreement is itself a home improvement contract subject to the deposit cap. The statute grants design authority for work the contractor will perform and supervise. No source of any tier answers the design only case. That is a question for a California construction attorney, and it is the single highest value unanswered question here.

The third finding that should change behaviour is about closeout, not sales. Two regulators, the state licensing board and the FTC, independently tell homeowners to collect at least three bids, check recent similar work, verify testimonials and get everything in writing. So every lead arrives inside a comparison the buyer has been coached to run. And when things go wrong, the licensing board's own numbers show that roughly half of the licensee complaints closed before any field investigation closed for insufficient evidence. Whoever holds the paperwork holds the advantage. That argues for dated substantial completion records, signed releases from subcontractors and suppliers, and photographs, more than it argues for any change to the website.

On money, the reliable numbers are about wages and prices, not about profit. Field wages in this metro area run about 23 percent above the national median for the same work, and a crew lead costs about 60 percent more per hour than a field hand. Consumer prices for gardening and lawncare services rose about 4.8 percent a year from 2019 to 2023, while the local all items index rose closer to 2 to 3.8 percent. A plain cost of living escalator in a maintenance agreement has been a real price cut for this trade. The state minimum wage rises every January on a published schedule, which argues for aligning maintenance renewals with the calendar year.

Geography is the other reliable lever. The routing mathematics is solid and old: doubling the number of stops inside the same service area cuts driving per stop by about 29 percent, and travel out from the yard grows faster with volume than travel between stops does. That is an argument for grouping stops by day and for treating distance from Redwood City as a separate pricing input from distance between clients. It is also why a single unqualified site visit is the worst trip the company makes, since it gets no density benefit at all.

Now the honest part. Almost nothing here is about a four person residential firm on the Peninsula. The census data confirms the shape of the business is normal, since about 63 percent of California landscaping employers have fewer than five people and 90 percent fewer than twenty, but every survey that reports profit, software use or close rates samples commercial contractors that are much larger, and most of those surveys are published by companies selling the software being measured. There is no independent measurement anywhere of whether buying a business management platform improves anything. The one vendor comparison that claims it does compares its own customers to non customers with no control for firm size, which is exactly the pattern selection alone would produce.

Several things people repeat as facts are folklore and should be treated that way. The typical design fee as a share of construction cost, the standard consultation charge, the share of firms that credit design toward construction, close rates by process, plant warranty norms, callback rates for landscape work, and drive time as a share of the crew day, none of these could be traced to any source that discloses how it was measured. In several cases the widely quoted numbers trace to cost aggregator pages or software marketing. They are not in this base and should not be added without a source that says who was asked and how.

The practical consequence is that a few decisions have to be settled with the company's own records rather than with research. Ninety days of logged leads with source, stated budget, whether a visit happened, hours and miles used, and outcome would settle the qualification question faster than any study. One month of truck GPS would produce a better drive time number than anything published. The company's own callback history over the last several years would settle the warranty question. Those measurements are cheap, and there is no published substitute for any of them.

themes.title: California law already writes most of the rules
themes.summary: The strongest and most transferable evidence in the set is statutory and regulatory, and it is specific to California residential work. Contract contents, the deposit ceiling, the cancellation window, the license number in advertising, and the narrow service and repair exception are all fixed by law rather than by preference. Two independent limitation clocks run behind them, four years on written contracts and ten years on latent defects, plus the licensing board's own separate discipline window.
themes.whatItMeansForGmz: Set the deposit, cancellation notice, change order rule and license number once, in one place, and treat them as compliance objects rather than copy. Date substantial completion on every job, because the ten year latent clock starts from documentary events. Do not publish a site wide payment schedule or lead time, because those are per job contract terms.

themes.title: The paid design step has a regulatory foothold and an unsettled legal edge
themes.summary: The state water ordinance turns a permit ready plan set into a required deliverable above 500 square feet of new landscape, and it lets a licensed landscape contractor sign the design plan, which is what makes an in house paid design step workable at four people. What no source resolves is whether a design only agreement the client may take elsewhere sits inside a contractor's licensing authority, or whether that agreement is itself a home improvement contract subject to the deposit cap.
themes.whatItMeansForGmz: Sell design as the regulated, signed, permit ready deliverable, and carry the third party irrigation audit cost in the estimate because the designer and installer cannot perform it. Get counsel to answer the design only question before the two agreement structure is leaned on harder, and add a limited licence clause covering what a client may do with a paid plan set.

themes.title: The buyer arrives inside a three bid comparison, and trusts what can be checked
themes.summary: Two regulators independently coach homeowners to collect several bids, compare like for like, check recent similar projects and verify testimonials. Separately, reviews are widely read but roughly half of readers doubt them, and endorsement rules require testimonials to be honest, current and typical. The things a firm can publish that reviews cannot supply are the checkable ones: a licence number, named towns, a written process.
themes.whatItMeansForGmz: Publish how scope is defined and what the design step contains, since comparability is what the buyer has been told to look for. Store an approval date beside the approved flag on testimonials and re confirm at intervals, and publish a representative spread of projects rather than only the smoothest ones.

themes.title: Documents decide disputes, and the disputes will be cosmetic
themes.summary: The largest handover defect study found no structural defects at handover and overwhelmingly surface, tolerance and functionality items, some surfacing only after the client lives with the work. California's licensing board resolves complaints at intake, where about half of the pre investigation closures were for insufficient evidence, and most single item landscape disputes fall under the mandatory arbitration ceiling. The state's own establishment definitions supply a defensible one year anchor.
themes.whatItMeansForGmz: Build a closeout packet around the state's own certificate of completion list, add a scheduled 30 to 60 day return visit, and collect statutory releases from every subcontractor and supplier. Write the warranty term with exclusions before any warranty language reaches the website, since advertising a guarantee requires publishing its limits alongside it.

themes.title: Recurring maintenance is a pricing and geography problem
themes.summary: Local wages, the trade's own price index and the routing mathematics all point the same way. Field labour here runs well above national, a crew lead costs about 60 percent more per hour than a field hand, gardening and lawncare service prices have outrun the local cost of living index, and doubling stop density in a fixed area cuts driving per stop by about 29 percent. Turnover, not headcount growth, is the structural labour problem.
themes.whatItMeansForGmz: A plain cost of living escalator is a below market escalator for this trade, so it needs a floor or an add on. Group stops by day so each truck makes one round trip from the yard, price distance from the yard separately from distance between clients, and align renewals with the January minimum wage step.

themes.title: Almost every number about the trade describes a bigger firm
themes.summary: Census data confirms a four to six person firm is the modal California landscaping business, but the surveys that report profit, software use, revenue mix and close rates sample commercial contractors with no small firm breakout, and most are published by companies selling what is being measured. The one benchmark that discloses its sample has 142 self selected firms nationally, which leaves very few cells comparable to a small coastal residential shop.
themes.whatItMeansForGmz: Treat any survey mean as describing the other half of the industry's money until it shows a size breakdown, and add roughly a fifth to a quarter to any national labour figure before it means anything locally. Use design build delivery research for its direction only, since it says schedule and accountability rather than lower price.

themes.title: Software: half the trade is not on a platform, and nobody has measured whether it helps
themes.summary: The adoption numbers come from vendors, the pricing tiers that matter are gated above the cheap entry prices, total cost of ownership cannot be computed for any vendor from public information, and two apparently independent shortlist names are now one company. The only outcome evidence is a vendor comparing its own customers with non customers and controlling for nothing.
themes.whatItMeansForGmz: Staying off a platform is not an outlier position. If job costing is the reason to buy, price the tier that actually includes it and confirm the tier boundary in writing, budget for an unquantified onboarding fee, and treat an auto renewing annual contract with 60 day notice as the real switching cost. No vendor is documented as modelling design sold as a share of construction, which has to be checked by product demonstration.

decisionTests.decision: No written workmanship warranty. Nothing published, nothing signed, the owner returns if something he installed fails.
decisionTests.plainAnswer: Two of the three arguments go your way, and the third one does not. Nobody can tell you what share of firms like yours put a term in writing, because that number does not exist in any source worth citing. Nobody can show you that a written warranty wins jobs either, so anyone promising it will lift your close rate is guessing. Where you are wrong is the legal reasoning. Staying silent does not shorten anything.
decisionTests.whatTheLawActuallyDoes: California's home improvement contract statute never uses the words warranty or guarantee, so what you offer is a business choice. But the contract itself must be written and signed, so the four year written contract clock is what runs, not the two year one for handshake deals. The four year cutoff for obvious defects is expressly switched off for owner occupied single family homes, which is most of your work. Buried work carries ten years. The licensing board has its own four and ten year window that nothing you sign can touch. So the unwritten position runs to the outer limits and defines nothing inside them.
decisionTests.recommendation: Write a one year workmanship term with explicit exclusions, and a separate one year plant establishment term with trees handled by trunk size or carved out. Anchor the numbers to Civil Code 896(g)(7) and (g)(12) and the state water ordinance establishment definition rather than trade folklore. Date substantial completion on every job. Have California counsel review it, and keep it off the website until the term, the exclusions and the duration all exist together, because advertising a guarantee obliges you to publish its limits.
decisionTests.costOfInaction: Every callback is negotiated from zero with a client you want to keep on the maintenance book, because nothing excludes under watering, freeze, rodent damage, third party alteration or lapsed maintenance. You cannot put a warranty reserve into an estimate for an obligation you have never defined, so callbacks come out of the current job's margin. And at the licensing board, where about half the complaints closed before investigation closed for insufficient evidence, these are decided on documents you do not have.
decisionTests.wouldChangeMyMind: Your own callback history. If the real rate of return and repair events over the last several years is close to zero, the exposure and reserve arguments shrink to noise and the answer becomes leave it verbal and document the closeout instead. Also a tiered survey of small residential contractors showing written terms are near universal here, which would harden the recommendation, or one showing written terms raise claim frequency, which would reverse it.

decisionTests.decision: No minimum project size and no starting price on the website. Callers find out on the phone whether they are in range.
decisionTests.plainAnswer: Nothing measures this. Not weak evidence, none. Every source that spoke to it directly was a lead vendor or a marketing agency. Anyone quoting a percentage for how much a published minimum cuts tire kickers is quoting a blog. Your own numbers are the only way to settle it.
decisionTests.whatTheNearestEvidenceSays: The best research on publishing prices at all comes from healthcare, and it found the tools are mostly ignored, with small effects among the few who use them. So a published number is a weak instrument either way. The more interesting result is that under price transparency the well regarded providers priced up rather than down. That route is closed to you right now, because the site's projects, photos and testimonials are still placeholders. A floor published above an empty portfolio is just a bare number.
decisionTests.recommendation: Keep the no published minimum for now, because spare capacity makes an unqualified visit nearly free and the market has been soft, but treat that as right for a reason that expires. As the next two or three real projects land, replace the silence with a coarse budget band on completed work plus a published fixed price and deliverable list for the design step. Never publish a company wide starting price, because price and dates are per job contract terms, and because the FTC requires a documented basis before an objective claim runs.
decisionTests.costOfInaction: Your buyers are told by both the licensing board and the FTC to collect at least three bids and compare like for like. You supply nothing comparable, so the comparison happens using the two firms that did say something, usually on price. All the qualification work stays on your phone and your windshield as an untracked tax. And the one route by which disclosure helps a good firm stays shut while the site is stubs.
decisionTests.wouldChangeMyMind: Ninety days logging every inbound lead: source, stated budget or refusal to state one, whether a visit happened, hours and miles used, outcome. Under about one in five out of range and short visits means drop the question. A third or more of your windshield time means a coarse published band pays for itself. Also note this flips when the book fills, so it needs a review date rather than standing as settled policy.

decisionTests.decision: Free site visit, plus a quick concept and a planning budget at no charge, bounded at about an hour of effort and scaled to property size.
decisionTests.plainAnswer: The free visit holds up. The free take away does not. How common it is to charge for a consultation, and what charging does to lead quality, are both unmeasured by any source worth citing, so nobody should tell you to start charging at the door, including me.
decisionTests.whyTheVisitIsFine: The credence goods research says the party who defines the problem controls the price, and that a homeowner who arrives with a confident wrong self assessment gets quoted the most. Getting on site early and free is how you become the one defining the scope. That is direction only, from taxi meters and laptop repairs, so no number transfers.
decisionTests.whyTheFreeConceptAndBudgetIsNot: A concept with a budget is a scope definition, and your own licensing board tells homeowners to obtain three comparable bids. You are solving the comparability problem for the buyer, for free, and handing the answer to two competitors who never left their yard. When the trade drafts around design work that was paid for, it attaches a limited licence restricting use to that project. Your free version carries none of that. The unpriced budget number is also an undocumented representation you will be held to.
decisionTests.onScaledToPropertySize: Wrong scalar. Design effort scales with how complicated the program is, not lot area. California hands you a better line: 500 square feet of new landscape, or 2,500 renovated, with a permit or plan check, triggers the regulated documentation package. Scaling free effort to property size puts your biggest giveaways on exactly the jobs where the paid design step is most defensible.
decisionTests.recommendation: Keep the site visit free. Stop handing over the written concept and the planning budget. End every visit either in a signed design agreement or in a declined lead, and answer price curiosity with a coarse budget band on completed projects rather than a job specific number produced in an hour. Remember the three business day cancellation window, five days for clients 65 and over, sits in front of any kitchen table signature anyway.
decisionTests.costOfInaction: You pay an owner hour plus a full single stop round trip from the yard, the worst travel to productive time ratio in the business with no route density benefit at all, roughly three times per job won. On the two that do not close you have also given a competitor your scope definition and your budget number. Your free hour is your only design sales capacity, so every unqualified trip is a paid design conversation you did not have.
decisionTests.wouldChangeMyMind: Thirty logged visits with lead source, whether a concept and budget were handed over, and whether a design agreement was signed. If cold web leads convert close to referrals, the free concept is doing real work. A six month test withholding the written concept while keeping the visit free would settle it directly. And if the maintenance book already supplies most design work, the question shrinks, because visits to known accounts are cheap and pre qualified.

gaps: Whether a design only agreement written by a licensed California contractor is a home improvement contract under B&P 7151.2, and so subject to the deposit cap and mandated contents. Unresolved by statute text and by any regulator guidance found. Requires a California construction attorney, not more research.

Whether B&P 7027.5's design authority reaches a design only engagement the client may take to another builder. The statute ties design to work the contractor performs and supervises. Sections 7027.1, 7027.3 and 16 CCR 832.27 were not read and should be, then reviewed by counsel.

Conflict between two verified California sources on when the three day cancellation right attaches. The licensing board conditions it on where the contract was negotiated; B&P 7159 states the notice as required contract content. Counsel should reconcile before any agreement form is standardised.

Typical design fee as a percentage of construction cost for residential landscape design build. Every figure located (10 to 20 percent, 6 to 15, 8 to 15) traces to cost aggregator or contractor marketing pages. Would require a trade survey with a disclosed sample, which does not appear to exist.
Whether initial consultations are charged, and typical amounts. No tiered source discloses it. The circulating $100 to $300 range traces to homeowner cost aggregator pages.
How common it is to credit a design fee toward construction. Genuinely unmeasured; no survey of any tier asks the question.

How common phased design agreements with explicit go or no go gates are in residential work. Unmeasured. The nearest analogue is capital project front end planning research on projects over $1.5 billion, whose magnitudes do not transfer.

The Project Definition Rating Index threshold of under 200 for adequate scope definition. Not present on the accessible CII page; the underlying report is paywalled. Requires buying RS213-1 or a CII implementation resource.

Close rates by process type in landscaping. The circulating 63 versus 38 percent same day estimate figures are unsourced and are not in the association report they are attributed to. The roughly 55 percent industry average traces to an outsourced finance firm's marketing page.
The value of qualifying leads before a site visit. No study of any tier quantifies it for residential contracting. Requires the firm's own ninety day lead log.

Whether publishing a minimum project size or a starting price changes the mix or quality of inbound leads for a residential contractor. Nothing at any tier. The only reliable route is to publish a minimum, tag leads before and after, and compare qualified lead rate over a fixed window.

Whether published FAQ or process content affects contractor selection or inquiry to consultation conversion. Appears unstudied for home services. Every inference here from regulator guidance to site content is an inferential leap and should be labelled as one.
Whether publishing a coarse budget band on a project page affects lead quality. Unevidenced. The healthcare price transparency literature is the nearest analogue and transfers poorly.

Whether disclosing design fee as a percentage of construction helps or hurts, which is how this firm sells design. No source at any tier addresses disclosure practice or buyer response for that structure.

How homeowners actually choose between competing residential bids. The peer reviewed contractor selection literature covers public and commercial procurement with formal weighted tender evaluation, a different buyer under different rules. One relevant ASCE paper returned HTTP 403 and was not read.

No California or Peninsula specific consumer research at any tier on how homeowners select landscape contractors or what they want to see before making contact. The licensing board brochure is prescriptive guidance, not consumer research. This is the largest transferability problem in the base.
No post 2015 tiered measurement of consumer trust in online reviews. The Pew data was fielded in late 2015, before the FTC's 2023 review manipulation rulemaking. Direction of any shift is unknown.

Section numbering in the adopted 2025 state water ordinance. The DWR PDF is a rulemaking redline carrying prior and adopted text, so applicability appears under both an old and a new section number. Any section cited to a client or agency should be confirmed against the codified 23 CCR text.

Adoption and effective dates of the water ordinance text used here. The PDF carries no adoption date on its face and interleaves 2015 and newly numbered sections, so which text governs a given job date is not resolvable from that file.

The new section 494 Certificate of Completion Package under the prescriptive and performance compliance options. Referenced in the adopted text but its body is absent from the fetched document. Confirm against the codified regulation before finalising a closeout packet.

Operative water ordinance thresholds in Redwood City, San Mateo County and neighbouring cities. Local agencies may adopt stricter ordinances, so the 500 and 2,500 square foot figures are a floor. Requires reading each local ordinance and its forms.
USDA hardiness zone for the actual towns served, which the caliper based tree establishment rule depends on. Confirm against the current USDA map before adopting a caliper based warranty term.
Local Peninsula minimum wage ordinances were not checked. Several San Mateo County cities exceed the state rate. Requires checking each city's ordinance directly.

Currency of several statutory texts. Pages for CCP 337.1, CCP 337.15, B&P 7091 and Civil Code 896 were fetched without capturing an enactment or amendment date, so those findings cannot show their own age.

The eCFR source notes for 16 CFR Parts 239 and 255 could not be read because the URL redirects to an interstitial. Part 255's 2023 revision date came from the FTC press release. Part 239 is cited undated.

Whether 16 CFR Part 239, the warranty advertising guides, applies to construction service warranties rather than consumer product warranties. Its own examples concern returning goods in original packaging. A California construction attorney is the right source.

Typical workmanship warranty terms offered by landscape contractors: no survey at any acceptable tier reports what share offer a written warranty or for how long. Everything located was anecdotal trade copy.

Plant establishment and replacement guarantee norms. The one year is standard claim cannot be traced to any source disclosing a sample or method. The one year figure surviving here rests on regulation, not on evidence of practice.

Callback and rework rates specific to landscape design build: nothing at any tier. All rework research covers vertical building construction. The firm's own callback history is the only available source.
Callback and rework economics for firms under about ten employees: nothing found. The rework literature samples large contractors and production builders.

Rework cost as a share of contract value. The 0.38 and 0.76 percent figures traced to a society news article with no disclosed sample and were dropped. The underlying peer reviewed study exists and should be obtained through a library.

Secondhand rework ranges of 2 to 6 percent and 3.15 percent appear in a literature review that was read directly, but neither original paper could be fetched. Recorded as unverified secondhand citations only.
The often quoted claim that rework averages 5 percent of total project cost was not confirmed against any primary publication and is not cited.

The relationship between documented handover and dispute frequency: no empirical study at any tier. The nearest proxy is the licensing board's insufficient evidence closure rate, which is suggestive rather than a study of the question.

Licensing board complaint data broken out by licence classification. The enforcement report does not disaggregate, so there is no California figure for complaints against C-27 landscaping contractors specifically.
Willingness to pay for a builder provided maintenance program: the full text returned HTTP 403, so the roughly $27 a month figure was struck. Requires library access to the article.
Whether offering a written warranty changes which contractor a homeowner hires. The only tiered study found measures stated willingness to pay for new home warranties, not selection.

Residential maintenance churn or retention rate: nothing at T1 or T2. The only candidates are commercial weighted trade press that could not be fetched. The firm's own account history over three years would answer it.

The break even between a price increase and the risk of losing a recurring account: no published empirical answer in any field service industry. Derivable from the firm's own gross margin per account and replacement acquisition cost, which is more trustworthy anyway.

Distribution of actual annual increases applied by landscape maintenance firms, and the retention effect of a given increase size. Unmeasured. The marketing literature establishes direction only and its sample sizes remain behind paywalls.

Drive time as a share of the landscape maintenance workday: no measured figure at any tier. The circulating wrench time benchmarks trace to field service software marketing. One month of truck GPS or timesheets would produce a better number than anything published.
Cost per stop as a function of route density in a real residential grounds maintenance operation. The routing literature is analytical or simulated and has never been calibrated on this trade.

Route density effect on the crew day rather than on driving. Every source addresses travel distance or time; none addresses the share of a crew day that is drive time, which is the ratio that decides whether density yields another billable stop.

No producer price index exists for landscaping services. The nearest output price measure, the gardening and lawncare consumer price item, is thinly published with no annual average after 2023, so the 4.8 percent escalation benchmark cannot be extended from a government source.

No Bay Area price index exists for landscape maintenance services specifically. Comparing the national gardening item against the local all items index mixes geographies and periods and is indicative only.

No survey at any tier isolates firms under twenty employees or under $1M revenue. The largest software surveys publish no size breakdown and sample commercial contractors; the one disclosed association sample of 142 firms is spread thin across bands and regions.

No independent, non vendor measurement of outcomes from business management platform adoption exists. No controlled study, no before and after design, no third party replication. Only a vendor comparing its own customers with non customers, uncontrolled for size.

No source at any tier reports failure or abandonment rates for business management software among small contractors, nor any switching cost figure: no implementation hours, migration cost, productivity loss or cost of a failed adoption. The only hard switching cost documented is one vendor's auto renewing annual contract with 60 day notice.

Total cost of ownership cannot be established for any vendor from public information. One onboarding fee is referenced but never quantified, another vendor's per user and implementation rates are unpublished and its tier prices contradict each other on its own page, a third publishes nothing, and every top tier is quote only.
One vendor's Grow tier price could not be pinned down: two direct fetches of the same page returned incompatible numbers. Must be confirmed directly from the vendor before any cost comparison.
One vendor's supposed $1M revenue entry point is not on its own page, which names no minimum, and traces only to a competitor's comparison page. Its real minimum viable customer size is undocumented.

No source addresses whether any platform models selling design as a separate paid step priced as a share of construction. This is arguably the most decision relevant software question and can only be answered by direct product evaluation.

No source directly measures whether firms keep a separate estimating tool alongside a platform. The tool count figures are the nearest proxy and do not name which categories are duplicated or separate platform users from non users.

The most quoted job costing statistic in the trade, 46 percent using job costing software alongside a 60 percent estimate accuracy figure, traces to a commissioned survey that does not disclose the landscape subset's sample or selection method. Not cited.

A digital adoption survey reporting that about half name training and implementation as the biggest barrier was rejected: it discloses a respondent count but nothing about selection, screening or field dates, and draws on the vendor's own customer base. The underlying idea, that implementation capacity rather than price decides success for a small firm, remains plausible and unevidenced.

Two trade publications' industry reports remain unfetchable, returning empty bodies on repeated attempts. Their circulating figures on technology reliance, retention, net margin and difficulty raising prices exist only in search extractions. Someone should open those pages in a real browser and read the methodology box.

One trade publication's service mix breakdown, showing design build offered by 62 percent of surveyed companies, discloses no sample size or recruitment method anywhere and fails even the lowest tier.

The remodelers' cost of doing business study segments design build against general remodelers, which would be the closest analogue to whether selling design separately pays, but no sample size is disclosed publicly and the segmentation is behind a paid publication.

The association's financial benchmark report is the one industry benchmark that discloses its sample and segments gross profit by design build versus maintenance, but those figures sit behind the paywall. If it is bought, read the respondent profile appendix first.

A consumer survey on homeowner use of lawn and landscape services could not be fetched from the primary source, which returned HTTP 403. Trade press discloses enough method to qualify it, but it is nine years old and measures service usage rather than published practice.

The advocacy summary attaching specific margins to the peer reviewed delivery study carries no publication date and its headline faster delivery figure is undefined on the page. It should not be quoted without the underlying foundation report.
Sample sizes for both cited marketing papers remain unknown. Publisher sites returned HTTP 403 or CAPTCHA. Only abstracts were reachable, so both support direction only, never a magnitude.
A cited restaurant rating study appeared only in search snippets; publisher pages returned HTTP 403 or no article content. Deliberately not cited.

The government bulk wage files are not retrievable from this environment, returning bot blocks on repeated attempts. All current wage figures were re sourced through the public data API. Anyone re verifying should use the API or a browser rather than command line downloads.

The entire labour cost section was anchored to a superseded wage release in earlier drafts. The current release moved the local premium over national from about 27 percent to about 23 percent and the crew lead premium from about 49 to about 60 percent. Any downstream calculation built on the older release needs re running.

No verified prior year California or national wage baseline exists here, because the state and national bulk files are blocked. The earlier California median figure could not be traced and was removed.

Structure of residential maintenance agreements: no T1 or T2 evidence on typical term length, cancellation notice or renewal mechanism. What exists is public agency commercial contracts, which are one sided by design, plus California statutory constraints. The gap between them is where this firm has to make its own policy choice.

Whether the automatic renewal law applies to a bespoke, in person signed residential service agreement with a licensed contractor is not settled by the bill text, and it was not checked for later amendments. Counsel should confirm before any auto renewing maintenance agreement is issued.

Licensing board consumer pages carry no publication or last updated date and cite no code sections, so their currency cannot be established from the page itself. The underlying statutes should be read directly before any guidance is relied on.
One board publication remains unreachable at its short URL, returning HTTP 404. The equivalent guidance is now sourced from the printed brochure, so nothing of substance is lost.

No T1 source exists for the software adoption question at all. Searches for peer reviewed or extension work on business management software among landscape contractors returned nothing landscape specific. Every adoption, pricing and outcome figure here is T2 or T3, and all but one T3 source is published by a company selling the software being measured.

No California or Peninsula specific data on contractor software adoption, pricing or practice exists at any tier. The census firm size data is the only California specific evidence in that section, and it says nothing about software.

Nothing in this base is specific to the San Francisco Peninsula, to four person firms, or to California landscape contractors as a class, outside the regulatory findings. Every quantitative finding is national, from another sector, or both, and none of the local ones is about sales process.

A note on tooling, recorded because an earlier audit reached conclusions by invoking it: the claim that PDF text extraction was broken in this environment is false. Extraction works, and the strongest finding in the set was recovered that way. Any earlier conclusion excused by broken PDF tooling should be re checked.

A gap closed and recorded so it is not reopened: the self diagnosis field experiment was previously listed as blocked by a paywall. A free full text working paper version exists, giving country, sample size and absolute effect. The paywall blocked only the journal version, not the evidence.

findings.claim: California law requires a home improvement contract and any changes to it to be in writing and signed, and dictates its contents, including the contractor's name, business address and license number, approximate start and completion dates, a description of the project and significant materials and equipment, progress payments stated in dollars and cents referencing the work performed, a mechanics lien warning and a three day (five day for seniors) right to cancel notice.
findings.figure: $500 aggregate contract price threshold
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7159 (California Legislative Information)
findings.bearsOn: Start dates, completion dates and payment schedules are per job statutory contract terms, so a site wide lead time or payment schedule creates a promise the contract must then honour job by job. Also applies to the design agreement if its price exceeds $500.
findings.caveat: Residential home improvement only, not commercial work. Amended by Stats. 2025 Ch. 585 Sec. 1.5 (SB 517) effective 1 January 2026, so any secondary summary written before 2026 may be out of date.

findings.claim: B&P 7159.5(a)(3) provides that if a downpayment is charged on a home improvement contract it shall not exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) or 10 percent of the contract amount, whichever amount is less, and that thereafter the contractor shall neither request nor accept payment that exceeds the value of the work performed or material delivered.
findings.figure: $1,000 or 10% of contract amount, whichever is less
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7159.5 (California Legislative Information)
findings.bearsOn: If a paid design step is folded into the construction contract the cap bites and no meaningful design fee can be collected up front. This is the structural reason a two agreement model is used in California.
findings.caveat: Merges two duplicate entries for the same statute. The 12 point boldface requirement is NOT in this section; it is in B&P 7159. A separate exception exists for contractors who file a blanket performance and payment bond with the Registrar, so never more than 10 percent is not universally true. Whether a design only agreement is itself a home improvement contract is unresolved.

findings.claim: B&P 7159 requires a home improvement contract to contain, in at least 12 point boldface type, the statement THE DOWNPAYMENT MAY NOT EXCEED $1,000 OR 10 PERCENT OF THE CONTRACT PRICE, WHICHEVER IS LESS, and a three business day notice of cancellation whose statutory text already permits cancellation by emailing, mailing, faxing or delivering a written notice, with a five day period for senior citizen buyers.
findings.figure: 12 point boldface; 3 business days; 5 days for seniors
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7159 (California Legislative Information)
findings.publishedDate: unknown (no amendment line surfaced in the fetched view)
findings.bearsOn: Whatever is signed at a kitchen table has prescribed contents and a prescribed cancellation notice. Email cancellation is already in the statute and need not be treated as a pending change.
findings.caveat: Created to hold the boldface requirement wrongly attributed elsewhere to 7159.5. The fetched view showed no amendment date, so the vintage of this text is unrecorded. Tension exists with the licensing board's conditional framing of the three day right; do not rely on either framing without counsel.

findings.claim: The licensing board states that unless the contract is negotiated at the contractor's place of business, and/or the contract price is under $25, the buyer qualifies for a three day right to cancel, with five days for buyers aged 65 and over from 2021 (AB 2471); and that the service and repair exception covers emergency repairs or services requested by the consumer on short notice, requires the contract be labelled a service and repair agreement, and caps total labour and materials under $750.
findings.figure: 3 business days; 5 days for buyers 65+; service and repair exception under $750
findings.sourceName: Contractors State License Board, Home Improvement Contracts, Warnings And Exceptions
findings.publishedDate: unknown (no publication or last updated date on the page)
findings.bearsOn: A design agreement signed at the end of a site visit sits inside a statutory cooling off period. A scheduled recurring maintenance visit is neither an emergency nor short notice, so the standard three day regime should be assumed for maintenance agreements.
findings.caveat: Merges two entries drawn from the same undated page. Regulator consumer guidance, not statute; it cites no code sections and its currency cannot be established from the page. Its conditional framing does not obviously match B&P 7159. It does not address recurring maintenance agreements as a category at all.

findings.claim: A maintenance or repair visit qualifies as a service and repair contract, escaping the full home improvement contract regime, only if all four conditions hold: the contract amount is $750 or less, the buyer initiated contact to request the work, the contractor does not sell goods or services beyond those reasonably necessary to take care of the particular problem, and no payment is due or accepted until the work is completed.
findings.figure: $750 or less
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7159.10 (California Legislative Information)
findings.bearsOn: Published copy promising that crews will spot opportunities and recommend upgrades on site, or any published prepayment terms, can defeat the buyer initiated and no advance payment conditions and pull routine visits into the full regime.
findings.caveat: The $750 ceiling is low against Peninsula labour costs, so many maintenance visits may already exceed it. Homeowners waive the three or five day cancellation right when signing a service and repair contract. Whether a given visit satisfies the four conditions is a legal judgement not made here.

findings.claim: Every California licensee shall include the license number in all construction contracts, subcontracts and calls for bid, and in all forms of advertising. A public website soliciting contracting work is advertising, so the license number is required on it.
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7030.5 (California Legislative Information)
findings.bearsOn: Makes the license number a compliance object rather than a trust badge. It must render on any page soliciting work, and holding it in one place is what stops a mistyped number appearing in three.
findings.caveat: The statute delegates detail to the registrar; placement, size and legibility regulations were not fetched. Treating a website as advertising is a reasonable reading, not a quoted holding, since the statute does not enumerate websites and no interpreting rule or case was retrieved.

findings.claim: California's four year outside limit on damage actions arising from patent construction deficiencies does not apply to an owner occupied single unit residence: subdivision (f) states that subdivisions (a) and (b) shall not apply to any owner occupied single unit residence.
findings.figure: 4 years (5 years maximum where injury occurs in year four); subdivision (f) exclusion
findings.sourceName: California Code of Civil Procedure § 337.1 (California Legislative Information)
findings.publishedDate: unknown (retrieved 2026-08-15; no amendment date in the fetched view)
findings.bearsOn: The one statutory cutoff that looks like a ceiling is expressly unavailable on owner occupied homes, which is most of a residential design build book. Sets the low end of the record retention horizon.
findings.caveat: Governs the enumerated damage actions arising from patent deficiencies. It is not a general bar on every theory a client might plead and does not displace the separate limitation on written contract claims. Amendment dates not captured.

findings.claim: No action may be brought to recover damages for a latent deficiency in the design or construction of an improvement to real property more than 10 years after substantial completion, with latent deficiency defined as one not apparent by reasonable inspection, and the period running from substantial completion but no later than final public agency inspection, recordation of a notice of completion, use or occupation of the improvement, or one year after termination of work, whichever comes first.
findings.figure: 10 years
findings.sourceName: California Code of Civil Procedure § 337.15 (California Legislative Information)
findings.bearsOn: The long tail on buried work: drainage, subsurface irrigation, footings, retaining walls and waterproofing behind hardscape. The trigger events are documentary, which is a direct reason to date and record substantial completion on every job.
findings.caveat: Does not apply to actions based on willful misconduct or fraudulent concealment, which removes the ten year protection entirely. The outside limit does not shorten any applicable shorter period that starts on discovery.

findings.claim: A complaint alleging a patent act or omission must be filed with the registrar within four years of the act, and a complaint alleging a latent act or omission pertaining to structural defects within 10 years, with the disciplinary action required within that same four or ten years or within 18 months of the filing of the complaint, whichever is later.
findings.figure: 4 years patent / 10 years latent structural, or 18 months from complaint filing, whichever is later
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7091 (California Legislative Information)
findings.bearsOn: Licence risk runs on its own clock, separate from civil liability. A client time barred in court may still be inside the regulator's window, so closeout files must survive on both clocks.
findings.caveat: The ten year limb is limited to latent acts pertaining to structural defects, not latent acts generally, and the 18 month tail is an alternative on a whichever is later basis, not an additional period. Governs discipline only; it creates no consumer right to repair or replacement.

findings.claim: California's home improvement contract statute prescribes required contents in detail, including approximate start and completion dates, a change order that becomes part of the contract only if in writing and signed before the covered work commences, the downpayment cap, the mechanics lien warning, licensing and insurance notices and the three day right to cancel, and the words warranty, warranties and guarantee do not appear anywhere in the section.
findings.figure: 0 occurrences of warranty, warranties or guarantee in BPC 7159
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7159 (California Legislative Information)
findings.bearsOn: Whatever warranty is offered is a commercial choice, not a compliance obligation, so it can be scoped, priced and limited deliberately. The written signed change order before work begins is the mandatory item that matters most at closeout.
findings.caveat: An absence claim resting on a full text word search of one section run twice. Related sections were not searched, and absence of a mandate is not absence of liability: implied warranty, breach of contract and negligence theories are unaffected.

findings.claim: Civil Code 896(g)(12) requires that landscaping systems be installed so as to survive for not less than one year and bars any action under that paragraph more than two years from close of escrow; paragraph (g)(7) requires irrigation systems and drainage to operate properly so as not to damage landscaping or other external improvements and bars action more than one year from close of escrow.
findings.figure: survive not less than 1 year; 2 year limit under (g)(12) and 1 year under (g)(7), both from close of escrow
findings.sourceName: California Civil Code § 896 (California Legislative Information)
findings.bearsOn: A California sourced anchor for a one year plant establishment guarantee and a matching one year irrigation and drainage term, instead of a number from trade folklore.
findings.caveat: Section 896 states the title applies to original construction intended to be sold as an individual dwelling unit, so it does not govern remodel and retrofit work on existing owner occupied homes. It transfers as a drafting benchmark only, and adopting it in a contract is what would make it enforceable against the firm.

findings.claim: Construction payment waiver and release forms must follow, substantially, one of the forms set forth in Civil Code sections 8132, 8134, 8136 and 8138 (conditional and unconditional on progress payment, conditional and unconditional on final payment); a conditional release is only binding if there is evidence of payment to the claimant; and paying the contractor or obtaining a release from the contractor does not guarantee that subcontractors and suppliers have been paid.
findings.figure: 4 statutory forms; Civil Code 8132, 8134, 8136, 8138
findings.sourceName: Contractors State License Board, Conditional and Unconditional Waiver and Release Forms
findings.publishedDate: unknown (no date on the page; fetched 2026-08-15)
findings.bearsOn: The backbone of a closeout packet: the applicable final payment release plus matching releases from every subcontractor and supplier on the job, which is the piece most small firms skip.
findings.caveat: Consumer facing guidance with no revision date. The page lists the four sections collectively without mapping each form to a section number, so the pairing should be read off the Civil Code itself.

findings.claim: The licensing board received 19,746 complaints in FY 2023/24, of which 15,165 were licensee complaints (13,791 filed by public consumers); of the 9,046 licensee complaints closed prior to referral for field investigation, 4,477 closed for insufficient evidence, 2,067 closed as settled in screening, 4 were sent to mandatory arbitration and 0 to voluntary arbitration.
findings.figure: 19,746 complaints received; 9,046 closed at intake; 4,477 insufficient evidence; 2,067 settled in screening; 4 mandatory arbitration; 0 voluntary
findings.sourceName: Contractors State License Board, FY 2023/24 Enforcement Annual Statistical Report
findings.sampleSize: 19,746 complaints; administrative census, not a sample
findings.bearsOn: Complaints settle or die at intake, which is exactly where a documented closeout file does its work. Roughly half of intake closures failed for insufficient evidence, so whoever holds records has the advantage.
findings.caveat: No breakout by licence classification, so there is no landscaping specific figure. Insufficient evidence closures favour whoever has documentation and cannot be read as vindication. Statewide totals say nothing about a small firm's complaint rate, and the counts mix in complaint types unrelated to warranty disputes.

findings.claim: The licensing board operates a mandatory arbitration program for disputes involving alleged damages of $25,000 or less and a voluntary arbitration program for disputes between $25,000 and $50,000, and warns that it cannot guarantee a consumer will get any money back and does not process claims against surety companies.
findings.figure: $25,000 or less mandatory; $25,000 to $50,000 voluntary
findings.sourceName: Contractors State License Board, Complaint Process Against Licensed Contractors
findings.bearsOn: Most single item landscape warranty disputes (a failed tree, a settled paver field, a controller) fall under $25,000, which is the mandatory band.
findings.caveat: The page carries no revision date, so currency cannot be established from it; confirm against the governing code sections before quoting to a client or writing into a contract. An arbitration being available says nothing about liability.

findings.claim: The licensing board's consumer brochure instructs California homeowners to get at least three contractor bids and references, to check each prospective contractor's recent similar projects, to take the time to get at least three identical bids and verify testimonials, to verify the licence number is current and in good standing, and to ensure all project materials and expectations are spelled out in a signed written contract including cleanup and debris removal.
findings.figure: at least three bids; licence required at $1,000 or more in combined labour and material
findings.sourceName: CSLB, What You Should Know Before Hiring A Contractor / Construction Project Checklist (publication 13P-078/0525)
findings.bearsOn: The California regulator telling actual buyers what to do before hiring, which doubles as a specification for site content: recent comparable projects, verifiable testimonials, the licence number. Confirms published content competes inside a three bid process.
findings.caveat: Prescriptive consumer guidance, not evidence about what homeowners actually do; nothing measures compliance. The May 2025 revision date is inferred from the publication code, as no explicit date is printed.

findings.claim: The FTC advises homeowners to get multiple estimates, states that a written estimate should include a description of the work to be done, materials, completion date and the price, tells them not to automatically choose the lowest bidder, and states that the contract should include the contractor's name, address, phone number and license number.
findings.sourceName: US Federal Trade Commission, Consumer Advice: How To Avoid a Home Improvement Scam
findings.bearsOn: An authoritative list of what the buyer has been coached to look for. Converging with the state regulator from an independent source is the strongest signal in this set: published content competes inside a multi bid process.
findings.caveat: Prescriptive guidance, not evidence about behaviour; no source found measures compliance. Two elements attributed to this page elsewhere, estimated start and completion dates and asking for an explanation where prices differ, could not be confirmed and were dropped.

findings.claim: The FTC requires an advertiser to hold a reasonable basis for an objective claim before the advertisement runs, not after: before a company runs an ad, it has to have a reasonable basis for the claims.
findings.sourceName: US Federal Trade Commission, Advertising FAQ's: A Guide for Small Business
findings.bearsOn: The regulatory version of the rule that undecided policy does not get published. An FAQ answer asserting a warranty term, a response time or a workmanship standard nobody has decided is an unsubstantiated objective claim.
findings.caveat: Plain language business guidance, not a statute or rule, and it does not bind a court. Substance dates to 2001 with only the editing recent. It applies to objective provable claims; the line against subjective puffery is not drawn precisely for service businesses.

findings.claim: If an advertisement mentions that a product comes with a guarantee or warranty, the ad should clearly disclose how consumers can get the details, and any conditions or limits on that guarantee or warranty must also be clearly disclosed in the ad.
findings.sourceName: US Federal Trade Commission, Advertising FAQ's: A Guide for Small Business
findings.bearsOn: A one line site claim such as all our work is guaranteed is not a safe simplification: it triggers an obligation to publish the limits and a route to the full terms alongside it.
findings.caveat: The source says a product, not a product or service. Extending it to a construction service warranty is an inference, and the underlying warranty guides are product focused. Substance dates to 2001.

findings.claim: 16 CFR § 239.3 requires that any material limitations or conditions attached to a Satisfaction Guarantee, Money Back Guarantee or similar representation be disclosed with clarity and prominence sufficient to be noticed and understood by prospective purchasers, and states that such terms should be used only when the seller refunds the full purchase price at the purchaser's request.
findings.sourceName: 16 CFR § 239.3, Guides for the Advertising of Warranties and Guarantees (Cornell LII)
findings.bearsOn: Constrains satisfaction style language specifically, the phrasing landscape firms reach for most often. The safer route is not to publish that language at all until callback window, covered workmanship and plant exclusions exist in writing.
findings.caveat: The section's examples are a 30 day return window and returning goods in original packaging, which is strong evidence Part 239 was not written for construction services. These are FTC guides, not a rule with independent penalties. No effective date is shown and the official copy could not be fetched, so currency is unverified.

findings.claim: Endorsements must reflect the honest opinions, findings, beliefs or experience of the endorser; advertisers are liable for misleading or unsubstantiated statements made through endorsements; and advertisers must have good reason to believe the endorser continues to subscribe to the views presented and remains a bona fide user, which requires checking at reasonable intervals.
findings.sourceName: 16 CFR § 255.1, Guides Concerning Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising (Cornell LII)
findings.bearsOn: An approval flag on a testimonial is a one time snapshot; this adds a continuing obligation. It argues for storing an approval date and re confirming at intervals, and means any factual assertion inside a quoted testimonial inherits the advertiser's substantiation burden.
findings.caveat: Part 255 comprises guides stating the Commission's enforcement views rather than independently enforceable rules. The 2023 revision date comes from the FTC press release and Federal Register listing, not from a source note, because the official page redirected to an interstitial.

findings.claim: Consumer endorsements must reflect the typical experience of consumers who use the product, not the experience of just a few satisfied customers, and disclaimers such as Not all consumers will get these results or Your results may vary are explicitly insufficient.
findings.sourceName: US Federal Trade Commission, Advertising FAQ's: A Guide for Small Business
findings.bearsOn: Governs which approved testimonials get published and how case studies are framed. A portfolio weighted toward the smoothest jobs can imply a typical experience the firm cannot deliver at scale.
findings.caveat: Substance dates to 2001. Enforcement attention has concentrated on health, weight loss and earnings claims; application to a small contractor's project gallery is untested and no enforcement action against a residential contractor on these grounds was located.

findings.claim: California's Model Water Efficient Landscape Ordinance applies to new construction landscape projects with a landscape area of 500 square feet or more and to rehabilitated landscape projects of 2,500 square feet or more, in each case where a building or landscape permit, plan check or design review is required; those projects must submit a Landscape Documentation Package.
findings.figure: 500 sq ft (new); 2,500 sq ft (rehabilitated)
findings.sourceName: California Department of Water Resources, Model Water Efficient Landscape Ordinance, final adopted text (23 CCR Div. 2 Ch. 2.7)
findings.bearsOn: Many Peninsula residential design build jobs cross 500 sq ft of new landscape, which makes a permit ready document set a regulatory deliverable rather than an upsell. It is the strongest available argument for charging for design as its own step.
findings.caveat: The PDF is a rulemaking redline carrying both prior and adopted text, so the thresholds appear under two section numbers; confirm any section cited against the codified 23 CCR text. Local agencies may adopt ordinances at least as effective as the model, so each Peninsula city must be checked individually.

findings.claim: MWELO § 492.6(b)(14) requires the landscape design plan to bear the signature of a licensed landscape architect, licensed landscape contractor, or any other person authorized to design a landscape, and § 492.6(b)(13) requires the statement I have complied with the criteria of the ordinance and applied them for the efficient use of water in the landscape design plan.
findings.sourceName: California Department of Water Resources, MWELO final adopted text, § 492.6(b)(13)-(14)
findings.bearsOn: The firm can sign the regulated deliverable itself rather than buying a landscape architect's stamp, which is what makes an in house paid design step viable at four people.
findings.caveat: The signature authority is bounded by the licensing statutes the section cross references and does not enlarge them. Section 492.8(a)(3) separately requires the grading design plan to bear the signature of a licensed professional as authorized by law, so a job needing grading and drainage plans is a different question with a different signer.

findings.claim: MWELO § 492.9(a) requires a Certificate of Completion with six elements: a project information sheet; certification by the signer of the landscape design plan, the signer of the irrigation design plan, or the licensed landscape contractor that the project was installed per the approved Landscape Documentation Package, with as built or record drawings where significant field changes were made and a hydrozone diagram kept with the irrigation controller; irrigation scheduling parameters; a landscape and irrigation maintenance schedule; an irrigation audit report; and a soil analysis report plus documentation verifying implementation of its recommendations. The applicant submits it to the local agency and ensures approved copies reach the local water purveyor and the property owner.
findings.figure: 6 required elements
findings.sourceName: California Department of Water Resources, MWELO final adopted text, § 492.9
findings.bearsOn: A regulator authored closeout list that can be adopted as the spine of a handover packet on every design build job, permitted or not. The as built requirement and the controller mounted hydrozone diagram are the two items small firms omit and later need.
findings.caveat: The six element list is at § 492.9; the newly numbered sections point to a § 494 Certificate of Completion Package whose body text is absent from the fetched document, so the current operative requirements should be confirmed against the codified text. Local agencies adopt their own versions and forms.

findings.claim: MWELO § 492.12 requires that all landscape irrigation audits be conducted by a local agency landscape irrigation auditor or a third party certified landscape irrigation auditor, and states that landscape audits shall not be conducted by the person who designed the landscape or installed the landscape; on large or multi installation projects an auditing rate of 1 in 7 lots, approximately 15 percent, satisfies the requirement.
findings.figure: third party auditor required; 1 in 7 lots (approximately 15%) on multi installation projects
findings.sourceName: California Department of Water Resources, MWELO final adopted text, § 492.12(a)-(b)
findings.bearsOn: A design build firm cannot sign off its own irrigation audit on a triggering job. A named third party certified auditor must be lined up and that cost carried in the estimate, or closeout stalls at the counter.
findings.caveat: Applies only where MWELO is triggered. Below threshold no audit is required, though a self performed commissioning check remains sensible. The auditor's credential should be checked against the ordinance's definition of a certified auditor.

findings.claim: MWELO defines establishment period of the plants as the first year after installing the plant in the landscape, or the first two years if irrigation will be terminated after establishment, adding that most plants are established after one or two years of growth and that native habitat mitigation areas and trees may need three to five years for establishment.
findings.figure: 1 year (2 years if irrigation is terminated after establishment; 3 to 5 years for trees and native habitat mitigation areas)
findings.sourceName: California Department of Water Resources, MWELO final text, definitions at § 490.2(a)(23) and § 491(q)
findings.bearsOn: A California regulator's own definition of establishment. It supports a one year plant guarantee as the default and gives a written basis for carving trees out to a longer or differently worded term.
findings.caveat: MWELO defines establishment for water efficiency purposes only. It does not create or imply a plant replacement guarantee and nothing in it obliges a contractor to replace a dead plant.

findings.claim: California Business & Professions Code 7027.5(a) states that a landscape contractor working within the classification for which the license is issued may design systems or facilities for work to be performed and supervised by that contractor.
findings.sourceName: California Business and Professions Code § 7027.5 (California Legislative Information)
findings.bearsOn: The statutory grant is worded around work the contractor will perform and supervise, so a design only product the client may take to another builder is at minimum not squarely inside those words. This is the statute the question turns on, not an answer to it.
findings.caveat: The conclusion that design authority is tied to building the job is an inference, not statutory text, and is deliberately excluded from the claim. Sections 7027.1, 7027.3 and the C-27 classification regulation were not read, any of which could bear on it. No legal opinion is offered or implied.

findings.claim: A 30 April 2013 DCA Legal Affairs Division memorandum concluded that B&P 5641 permits an unlicensed person to prepare only conceptual design drawings and planting plans for a single family dwelling, and that preparing construction documents, details or specifications for landscape features is landscape architecture requiring licensure or an exemption even where no local ordinance requires a licensed professional.
findings.sourceName: DCA Legal Affairs Division memorandum to the Landscape Architects Technical Committee, Section 5641 - Exceptions
findings.bearsOn: Where the line falls between a conceptual deliverable and a construction document deliverable, which is the natural gate for a phased design agreement. The concept to construction documents ladder is a licensing question, not only a pricing one.
findings.caveat: Addresses what an unlicensed person may do and says nothing about a licensed contractor's separate authority under 7027.5, which is the exemption actually relied on. It is non binding staff counsel advice, not law, and is 13 years old. The document is stamped confidential and privileged yet posted publicly, so its status as citable guidance is itself uncertain.

findings.claim: For contracts entered into, amended or extended on or after 1 July 2025, California's amended Automatic Renewal Law requires an annual reminder notice disclosing the product or service, the frequency and amount of charges and the means to cancel, and requires that cancellation be available in the same medium the consumer used in the transaction or the same medium in which the consumer is accustomed to interacting with the business; a voicemail cancellation request must within one business day be either processed or returned by a call back.
findings.figure: effective for contracts entered, amended or extended on or after 2025-07-01
findings.sourceName: California Legislature, AB 2863 (2023-2024), amending Business and Professions Code §§ 17601 and 17602
findings.bearsOn: If a maintenance agreement auto renews annually, this governs the renewal notice and the cancellation route. It rules out a renewal design depending on the client failing to notice and argues for an explicit annual re signing conversation, which is also the natural moment to apply the year's increase.
findings.caveat: Whether a bespoke, in person signed residential service agreement with a licensed contractor is an automatic renewal or continuous service offer at all is not settled by the bill text; the law was written with consumer subscriptions in mind. Later amendments superseding AB 2863 were not checked.

findings.claim: A current California public agency landscape maintenance contract uses a three year initial term with unilateral one year renewals held by the client, an asymmetric seven day termination for convenience available only to the client, and a CPI escalator capped at 5 percent that begins only after the initial term, with adjustment requests confined to a 1 March to 1 April window and failure to request by 1 April waiving that year's adjustment.
findings.figure: 3 year term plus up to three 1 year renewals at the client's option; 7 day termination for convenience; escalation deferred to year four, capped at 5%; 30 day request window with waiver
findings.sourceName: City of Upland, California, Landscape Maintenance Services Agreement with Mariposa Landscapes, Inc. (executed public contract, 42 pp.)
findings.sampleSize: n/a — a single contract, not a survey
findings.geography: California (City of Upland, San Bernardino County)
findings.bearsOn: A concrete template for how a sophisticated buyer structures recurring grounds maintenance. Each term is something to negotiate rather than accept if bidding public or HOA work, and the waiver trap is worth noting: the contractor loses its increase entirely by missing a 30 day window.
findings.caveat: T1 here reflects an authenticated public record, not research. It is evidence of one buyer's practice, not prevalence, and is drafted by the buyer's counsel under competitive bidding obligations, so it does not transfer to a residential agreement. Its index is a Southern California area series, not a Bay Area one. The cap and deferral are buyer favourable and should not be copied.

findings.claim: In the San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont, CA metro area, which contains Redwood City and all of San Mateo County, the median hourly wage for Landscaping and Groundskeeping Workers was $23.10 and the 75th percentile $28.87 in May 2025, across 12,270 workers.
findings.sourceName: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, May 2025, via the BLS Public Data API v2 (SOC 37-3011, area 0041860)
findings.sampleSize: n/a — establishment survey pooled over six semiannual panels
findings.bearsOn: The market wage floor under every maintenance stop. Any per crew day or per visit price has to clear a burdened rate built on roughly $22 to $29 an hour of straight wage before burden, overhead and profit.
findings.caveat: BLS warns these estimates are not designed for year to year comparison, so the small nominal drop from the prior release must not be read as a wage cut. OEWS is weighted toward larger employers, is not a rate card, and excludes owner draw and 1099 labour. San Mateo County pay may run above the MSA median, which is pulled down by outer East Bay counties.

findings.claim: Bay Area landscaping labour costs about 23 percent more per hour than the national median for the same occupation and about 5 percent more than the California median, and a crew lead in this metro costs about 60 percent more per hour than a field hand.
findings.figure: May 2025 SOC 37-3011 hourly median: metro $23.10 vs national $18.82 (+22.7%); vs California $21.90 (+5.5%). SOC 37-1012 supervisors: metro median $37.02/hr, employment 1,570; national $28.09/hr. Supervisor vs field hand +60.3%
findings.sourceName: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, via BLS Public Data API v2
findings.geography: US national and California vs San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont MSA
findings.bearsOn: Quantifies why any national benchmark on cost per stop or labour share understates this market. A national figure needs roughly a 20 to 25 percent uplift on the labour line, and a crew lead hour should be costed at roughly 1.6 times a field hour.
findings.caveat: The premium is on the wage line only. It says nothing about whether Peninsula clients pay a matching premium, which is the actual margin question. Prior release figures (+26.6% and +49%) should not be reused. Bulk BLS files returned bot blocks, so all figures came through the API.

findings.claim: National employment of landscaping and groundskeeping workers is projected to grow 4 percent from 2024 to 2034 (+42,400 jobs), while the broader grounds maintenance occupation group is projected to see about 171,600 openings a year, so annual hiring demand is roughly four times the net growth and is overwhelmingly replacement, not expansion.
findings.figure: Landscaping and groundskeeping: 1,192,500 (2024) to 1,235,000 (2034), +42,400, +4%. Grounds maintenance group: 1,296,400 jobs, ~171,600 annual openings; median pay $38,470/yr ($18.50/hr), May 2024
findings.sourceName: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook, Grounds Maintenance Workers
findings.bearsOn: The gap between 4 percent net growth and 171,600 annual openings is turnover. Crew churn, not headcount growth, is the structural labour problem, which makes route stability and a retained bilingual crew an asset worth protecting.
findings.caveat: The openings figure belongs to the broader grounds maintenance group, not the landscaping subset; the two populations must be kept separate. National only, saying nothing about Peninsula labour supply. The handbook median mixes in lower wage regions.

findings.claim: 94.3 percent of US landscaping services employer firms have fewer than 20 employees (108,274 of 114,842), but those firms hold only 44.0 percent of industry employment (340,782 of 774,028) and 48.3 percent of receipts ($57.13B of $118.36B).
findings.sourceName: US Census Bureau, Statistics of U.S. Businesses 2022, NAICS 561730 Landscaping Services
findings.sampleSize: n/a — full count administrative tabulation covering 114,842 employer firms
findings.bearsOn: The yardstick to hold every vendor and trade survey against. Any survey of commercial landscape professionals reporting a mean is describing the other half of the money.
findings.caveat: Counts employer firms only and excludes non employer sole proprietors, so the true share of tiny operators is higher. 2022 reference year, four years old, and receipts refresh only in economic census years.

findings.claim: A four to six person landscaping firm is the modal California landscaping business: 62.9 percent of California's landscaping services employer firms have fewer than five employees and 90.2 percent have fewer than twenty; firms under 20 employees hold 31.5 percent of the state's industry employment, and sub 20 employee firms average roughly $553,000 in annual receipts each.
findings.figure: 9,078 CA employer firms; 5,714 (62.94%) under 5 employees; 8,189 (90.21%) under 20; 32,255 of 102,414 employees (31.50%) in sub 20 firms; $4,527,969K receipts / 8,189 firms = $552,932 mean
findings.sourceName: US Census Bureau, Statistics of U.S. Businesses 2022, NAICS 561730, California
findings.sampleSize: n/a — administrative universe of employer firms
findings.bearsOn: Establishes the peer set and the revenue scale any software or overhead decision has to be affordable against. Any benchmark whose respondents skew above twenty employees is describing the top 10 percent of California firms by count.
findings.caveat: Merges two duplicate entries from the same source file. The ~$553K figure is arithmetic on two published cells, not a Census statistic; it is a mean of a heavily right skewed distribution, so the median firm is materially smaller, and Bay Area receipts per firm likely run above the state mean. Employer firms only. The Business Register assigns one NAICS per firm, so design build heavy firms may be classified elsewhere.

findings.claim: California landscaping firms with fewer than five employees book far more revenue per employee than firms with five to nine, and run a payroll to receipts ratio about eight points lower, which is consistent with the smallest firms carrying uncounted owner labour rather than being genuinely more productive.
findings.figure: Under 5 employees: $173,392 receipts per employee, payroll 23.15% of receipts, $298,202 receipts per firm. 5-9 employees: $126,853 receipts per employee, payroll 31.31% of receipts, $837,853 receipts per firm. All CA firms: $137,151 per employee, payroll 36.86% of receipts
