findings.sourceName: US Census Bureau, Statistics of U.S. Businesses 2022, ratios computed from published FIRM, EMPL, PAYR and RCPT fields
findings.bearsOn: A crossing point to watch when growing: the step from under five to five plus employees is where payroll as a share of receipts jumps 8.2 points. Adding a crew without adding route density or price produces this shape of margin compression.
findings.caveat: Derived ratios, not published statistics, and the uncounted owner labour reading is an inference. Payroll excludes S corp owner distributions and subcontract labour, both of which distort the smallest band in exactly the direction that produces this pattern. Receipts include materials pass through.

findings.claim: Consumer prices for gardening and lawncare services rose about 4.8 percent a year compounded from 2019 to 2023 on annual averages, well above general inflation, so a maintenance book held flat loses real value quickly.
findings.figure: CPI-U US city average, gardening and lawncare services (CUUR0000SEHP02): annual average 205.292 (2019) to 247.805 (2023), +20.71%, a 4.82% compound annual rate
findings.sourceName: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index series CUUR0000SEHP02
findings.sampleSize: n/a — thinly and intermittently sampled CPI item
findings.bearsOn: The empirical benchmark for an annual escalation clause. An escalator below roughly 4 to 5 percent a year has, over 2019 to 2023, been a real price cut for this service category.
findings.caveat: The series has publication gaps: zero observations in 2022 and no annual average published for 2024 or 2025, so it cannot be extended past 2023 and must not be annualised across the missing year. US city average only, with no Bay Area breakout, and the window is now three years stale with no way to extend it.

findings.claim: A cost of living escalator tied to the Bay Area all items index would have delivered only about 2.2 to 3.8 percent a year recently, below the increase in gardening and lawncare service prices, so a plain CPI clause is a below market escalator for this trade.
findings.figure: CPI-U San Francisco area all items (CUURS49BSA0): annual average 348.417 (2024) to 356.005 (2025), +2.18%; June 2025 356.460 to June 2026 369.913, +3.77%; 2019 to 2025 six year CAGR 3.18%
findings.sourceName: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index series CUURS49BSA0
findings.bearsOn: If a cost of living index is written into a maintenance agreement, this is what it actually pays out. It has run roughly 1 to 2.5 points a year below the trade's own price index, so a plain clause needs a floor, an add on, or a labour index alternative.
findings.caveat: The series is bimonthly, not monthly. All items CPI is a consumer basket dominated by shelter, not a cost index for a labour intensive field service. The comparison against the gardening item crosses two geographies and two end years, so the spread is indicative, not a measured gap.

findings.claim: California's statewide minimum wage is indexed to inflation and rises every January: $16.90 effective 1 January 2026 and $17.40 effective 1 January 2027, a 2.96 percent step.
findings.figure: $16.90/hr from 2026-01-01; $17.40/hr from 2027-01-01 (+$0.50, +2.96%); certified by the Department of Finance 31 July 2026
findings.sourceName: California Department of Industrial Relations news release 2026-66, corroborated by the DIR Minimum Wage page
findings.bearsOn: A dated, certain input for the annual maintenance repricing cycle. The floor moves every 1 January, which argues for aligning maintenance renewal and escalation dates with the calendar year rather than each account's anniversary.
findings.caveat: The 2.96 percent is arithmetic on the two published rates, not a figure the regulator published. Local Peninsula ordinances can set rates above the state figure and were not checked. The state minimum is not the binding wage here, since the local 25th percentile for this occupation is well above it.

findings.claim: Local travel distance per stop falls with the square root of stop density: doubling the number of stops inside a fixed service area cuts local travel distance per stop by about 29 percent, and quadrupling it halves per stop travel.
findings.figure: Optimal tour length approximated by k·sqrt(T·N), so travel per stop is proportional to sqrt(T/N). Doubling N: 29.3% reduction. Quadrupling N: 50.0%
findings.sourceName: Ansari, Basdere, Li, Ouyang & Smilowitz, Advancements in Continuum Approximation Models for Logistics and Transportation Systems 1996-2016, arXiv:1706.05448, eq. (7), citing Beardwood, Halton & Hammersley (1959) and Daganzo (2005)
findings.bearsOn: The mathematical case for geographic discipline in the maintenance book. The payoff to clustering is real but sublinear, so a scattered account that forces the service area open is expensive in a way a per visit price rarely recovers.
findings.caveat: Asymptotic, assuming roughly uniform scatter in a compact region; the paper warns the constant likely underestimates tour length for finite irregular regions. Real routes face street networks, traffic and fixed on site time, so the 29 percent applies to the driving component only, never to a crew day. Preprint, not the version of record.

findings.claim: Route cost decomposes into two terms that behave differently: yard to route line haul scales linearly with the number of stops served, while travel between stops scales only with the square root, so distance from the yard is punished much harder by growth than spread within the route is.
findings.figure: Total expected all vehicle travel distance approximated by 2r(v/V)·N + k·sqrt(T·N) (eq. 8), where r is depot to region distance and N is customers
findings.sourceName: Ansari, Basdere, Li, Ouyang & Smilowitz, arXiv:1706.05448, eq. (8), continuum approximation for the VRP after Daganzo
findings.bearsOn: Argues for grouping maintenance stops by day so each truck makes one round trip from the yard per day, and for treating distance from the yard as a separate pricing input from distance between stops. A one off site visit is a pure line haul trip with N of 1, the worst travel ratio in the business.
findings.caveat: The capacity framing maps imperfectly onto maintenance, where the binding constraint is crew hours rather than truck capacity, so the demand term has to be read as visits per truck day, an analogy rather than a result the paper supports. Preprint.

findings.claim: Published route optimization work in a stop collection setting reports a 14 percent reduction in total distance travelled, but from simulation against a naive baseline rather than from a measured field deployment.
findings.figure: 14% reduction in total distance travelled, in simulations of 8 to 20 collection points, versus algorithms optimized for single parameters
findings.sourceName: Ali, Javed, Alharbi, Alotaibi & Alkhathami, Internet of Things-Assisted Vehicle Route Optimization for Municipal Solid Waste Collection, Applied Sciences 14(1):287
findings.sampleSize: n/a — simulation, 8 to 20 bins per scenario
findings.bearsOn: Sets a realistic ceiling on what resequencing an existing route buys: low double digit percentage of the driving, not of the crew day. Useful mainly as a sanity check against vendors claiming 20 to 30 percent operational savings.
findings.caveat: Simulation only, in municipal waste collection, against a single parameter algorithm rather than an experienced dispatcher, so it almost certainly overstates the gain over a route a crew lead already knows. Treat as an upper bound on vendor claims and nothing more.

findings.claim: In credence goods markets, buyers who cannot signal familiarity with the service are overcharged far more often than buyers who can. In an Athens taxi field experiment, foreign passengers unable to signal knowledge of the tariff system were overcharged in 23 percent of rides versus 6 percent for Greek passengers.
findings.figure: 23% vs 6% overcharging rate
findings.sourceName: Kerschbamer & Sutter, The Economics of Credence Goods: a Survey of Recent Lab and Field Experiments, CESifo Economic Studies 63(1), reporting Balafoutas et al.
findings.sampleSize: 348 undercover taxi rides covering 4,400 km, GPS tracked
findings.bearsOn: Landscape design build is a textbook credence good: the homeowner cannot verify what was needed even after the work is done. Publishing how work is scoped and priced moves an inbound lead out of the uninformed category, and sells against rivals who profit from opacity.
findings.caveat: Athens taxi rides are short, low value, one shot transactions with a posted tariff and an anonymous seller, so the magnitude almost certainly does not transfer even if the direction does. This is a finding about seller behaviour, not about publishing: no arm tested published information, so the link to a website is an analogy. Nine years old.

findings.claim: Where sellers hold the expertise, institutions that make the seller liable for delivering what was needed outperform institutions that merely let the buyer verify what was done. In laboratory experiments, liability produced 82 percent of possible trades and 84 percent efficiency, while verifiability produced 50 percent of trades and only 16 percent efficiency.
findings.figure: liability 82% trade / 84% efficiency vs verifiability 50% trade / 16% efficiency
findings.sourceName: Kerschbamer & Sutter, CESifo Economic Studies 63(1), reporting Dulleck, Kerschbamer & Sutter
findings.geography: laboratory; country not stated in the survey article
findings.bearsOn: A design principle for what to publish: something the firm is bound by, such as a fixed design fee, a defined deliverable or a stated callback commitment, rather than information the buyer is expected to check. It also supports selling design as a separate signed agreement, which is itself a liability instrument.
findings.caveat: Abstract laboratory framing with typically student subjects, not contractors or homeowners. The percentages are experimental outcomes under an induced payoff structure and carry no meaning as business metrics; they must never be published or quoted as expected results. Verifiability began at 63 percent and decayed, so the headline contrast overstates the immediate gap.

findings.claim: A consumer volunteering their own diagnosis of the problem does not lower the price they are quoted. In a natural field experiment in the German computer repair market, a correct self diagnosis did not reduce the repair price relative to simply asking for a repair, while an incorrect self diagnosis more than doubled the average price.
findings.figure: incorrect self diagnosis more than doubled the average price; correct self diagnosis had no price reducing effect
findings.sourceName: Kerschbamer, Neururer & Sutter, Credence goods markets and the informational value of new media: A natural field experiment, Max Planck Institute for Research on Collective Goods Discussion Paper 2019/3
findings.sampleSize: 71 observations in wave 1 (24 baseline, 24 correct self diagnosis, 23 incorrect)
findings.bearsOn: Cuts against web forms that ask the homeowner to specify their own scope. It argues for capturing the problem and the site conditions rather than inviting the buyer to prescribe the solution, and for presenting the paid design step as the mechanism that replaces guesswork.
findings.caveat: Power is the decisive limit: the doubling rests on 23 observations in one arm, and the absolute difference is about 50 Euro, so it is a doubling of a small number. The setting is a low value one off repair of a deliberately manipulated laptop, not residential construction. Direction informative, magnitude not transferable.

findings.claim: Published price information changes far less buyer behaviour than expected, mainly because very few buyers look at it. A systematic review of 18 studies found low usage of price transparency tools to be a critical limiting factor, and that among those who had access to and actually used the tools, average total payments decreased by 1.6 percent; higher ranked providers captured a reputation premium that partially or fully offset the policy effect, while lower ranked facilities faced downward price pressure.
findings.figure: 18 studies from 2,157 records screened; 1.6% reduction among tool users; top ranked nursing homes 4.8 to 6.0% price increase over bottom ranked
findings.sourceName: Chen & Miraldo, The impact of hospital price and quality transparency tools on healthcare spending: a systematic review, Health Economics Review
findings.sampleSize: 18 studies in final synthesis, screened from 2,157 records
findings.bearsOn: The most rigorous evidence on whether publishing prices changes anything, and it counsels modest expectations. The reputation premium result suggests published pricing is a positioning instrument for a firm with a strong portfolio, and supports a coarse band over a precise price.
findings.caveat: Healthcare, where a third party usually pays, procedures are standardised and the tools were insurer or government portals rather than a contractor's own site. The 1.6 percent is conditional on having used a tool, so it is not an average treatment effect. The reputation premium is nursing home specific. Direction suggestive, magnitude does not transfer.

findings.claim: In FHWA's congressionally mandated Design-Build Effectiveness Study, design build project managers estimated an average -14.1 percent change in project duration, -2.6 percent in project cost and 0.0 percent in quality; across eleven matched project pairs, design build total duration ran 4.2 percent under plan while design bid build ran 4.8 percent over, but design build cost growth was 7.4 percent against design bid build's 3.6 percent.
findings.figure: -14.1% duration (62 responses); -2.6% cost (48); 0.0% quality (61); matched pairs -4.2% vs +4.8% duration, +7.4% vs +3.6% cost growth
findings.sourceName: US DOT Federal Highway Administration, Design-Build Effectiveness Study, Exhibit IV.12
findings.sampleSize: 29 agencies; 69 completed projects; 11 matched pairs; 48-62 responses per estimate
findings.bearsOn: The honest framing for design build to a client: schedule compression and single point accountability, not lower price. The matched pair cost result actively contradicts a cheaper build pitch.
findings.caveat: Roughly 20 to 25 years old. The headline percentages are project managers' subjective estimates on surveys, not measured outcomes, and FHWA says the 11 pair sample may not be statistically representative. Public highway procurement bears no resemblance to a residential yard; only the directional argument transfers.

findings.claim: A 212 project regression study found design build projects were delivered faster and with lower cost growth and schedule growth than construction manager at risk or design bid build, with design build unit cost comparable to design bid build, while except for delivery speed the gap in performance between the three methods has narrowed over time.
findings.figure: 212 projects
findings.sourceName: Roberts & Franz, Revisiting project delivery system performance from 1998 to 2018, Journal of Construction Engineering and Management (summary page, University of Florida Collaborative Project Delivery Lab)
findings.bearsOn: The best peer reviewed evidence that the design build delivery model itself is associated with better cost and schedule outcomes. This is the citation to use if the model ever needs defending in writing.
findings.caveat: What was read is the university lab's summary page, not the article, so the claim rests on a secondhand abstract. The sample is commercial and institutional buildings, majority public sector; a residential landscape job is outside the population entirely. Data to 2018, and the paper's own hedge means older larger claimed margins should not be quoted.

findings.claim: A peer reviewed analysis of 52,552 handover defects in 2,179 flats across 16 developments found no structural defects at handover; defects were dominated by surface appearance (64.5 percent), tolerance errors (9.3 percent) and affected functionality (6.8 percent), concentrated in internal walls, windows and mechanical and electrical systems, and some defects are not resolved until customers complain after first occupying the dwelling.
findings.figure: 52,552 defects across 2,179 flats in 16 developments; 64.5% surface appearance, 9.3% tolerance errors, 6.8% affected functionality
findings.sourceName: Forcada, Macarulla, Gangolells & Casals, Handover defects: comparison of construction and post-handover housing defects, Building Research & Information 44(3), 279-288 (author postprint)
findings.sampleSize: 52,552 defects in 2,179 dwellings across 16 developments, all built by one main contractor
findings.bearsOn: Tells a walkthrough punch list where to look. Callbacks are overwhelmingly appearance and tolerance items, not structural ones, and some only appear once the client lives with the work, which argues for a scheduled 30 to 60 day return visit rather than a single handover walk.
findings.caveat: All dwellings were built by the same main contractor, which the authors flag as a limit on representativeness. Spanish multi family flats differ substantially from Peninsula residential exterior work, and no landscape or hardscape category appears in the data. The pattern transfers; the percentages do not.

findings.claim: Trees provided with regular irrigation through the first growing season after transplanting require approximately three months per inch of trunk diameter to establish in USDA hardiness zones 9 to 11, six months per inch in zones 7 to 8, and one year or more per inch in zones 2 to 6, with desert climates requiring longer.
findings.figure: about 3 months per inch of trunk diameter in USDA zones 9 to 11
findings.sourceName: Edward F. Gilman, UF/IFAS Landscape Plants: Establishment Period for Trees
findings.geography: US national, expressed by USDA hardiness zone
findings.bearsOn: Converts a flat warranty term into a defensible rule. A 2 inch caliper tree needs roughly six months to establish and a 4 inch specimen roughly a year, so a flat 12 month guarantee is generous on small stock and thin on large specimen trees.
findings.caveat: Six years old, from a Florida land grant institution, so Peninsula summer dry conditions and the absence of summer rainfall are not modelled. The hardiness zone for the specific towns served must be confirmed first. It describes root establishment biology, not survival probability, and says nothing about shrubs, perennials or grasses. No sample size or trial data given.

findings.claim: The 2025 Financial Benchmark Report, compiled by Industry Insights from confidential surveys submitted by 142 organizations representing 344 locations covering FY2024, reports that the typical company saw 8.5 percent sales growth in 2024 versus 15.7 percent in 2022, a 13 percent median change in contract value per installation job and a median customer count up 13 percent to 355 clients per firm, and breaks gross profit out by work type including design build, with breakdowns by revenue size, profitability and region.
findings.figure: 142 organizations / 344 locations; 8.5% sales growth (typical company); +13% median contract value per installation job; 355 median clients
findings.sourceName: National Association of Landscape Professionals, Financial Benchmark Report announcement (data collected by Industry Insights)
findings.sampleSize: 142 organizations representing 344 locations, FY2024 data, confidential surveys
findings.bearsOn: The only landscape industry benchmark located that discloses its sample and segments gross profit by design build versus maintenance. If an outside yardstick is wanted for the two service lines, this is the one worth buying into and participating in.
findings.caveat: Merges two duplicate entries describing the same report. 142 self selected firms nationally, skewed toward companies large enough to submit full financial statements, so not a probability sample; a four person Peninsula firm will land in a thin or absent cell. The design build gross profit figures are behind the paywall and unseen, so nothing about design build margins can be quoted from it. The 8.5 percent is quoted as the typical company, not explicitly a median. An assertion elsewhere that firms above $10M performed strongest is unsupported by the page.

findings.claim: Construction Industry Institute research summary RS213-1 reports that projects with better aligned teams during front end planning performed approximately 10 percent better on costs and over 16 percent better on schedules.
findings.figure: ~10% better cost; >16% better schedule
findings.sourceName: Construction Industry Institute, Front End Planning: Break the Rules, Pay the Price (RS213-1)
findings.sampleSize: 17 case studies from projects over $1.5B; sample behind the 10%/16% figures not disclosed
findings.bearsOn: The nearest evidence for a phased design agreement with a scope definition gate before construction is authorised: define scope to a standard, then commit. It is the reasoning behind charging for the definition phase separately.
findings.caveat: Twenty years old, with no sample size disclosed behind the two headline percentages. The population is industrial and capital projects worth over $1.5 billion. The mechanism may transfer to a residential yard; the magnitudes must not be quoted as though they do. A Project Definition Rating Index threshold attributed to this page could not be found on it and is recorded as a gap.

findings.claim: Online reviews are widely consulted but only about half of readers believe them: 82 percent of US adults say they at least sometimes read online customer ratings or reviews before purchasing items for the first time, with 40 percent doing so always or almost always; among those who read online reviews, 51 percent say they generally give an accurate picture of product quality, while 48 percent say it is often hard to tell whether online reviews are truthful and unbiased.
findings.figure: 82% read at least sometimes; 40% always/almost always; among review readers, 51% accurate vs 48% hard to tell
findings.sourceName: Pew Research Center, Online reviews and ratings, in Online Shopping and E-Commerce
findings.sampleSize: 4,787 American Trends Panel respondents; margin of error ±1.94 percentage points
findings.bearsOn: Explains why a contractor's own published content still matters in a review dominated market. The things a firm can publish that reviews cannot supply are the independently checkable ones: a licence number, named towns, a written process, references on request.
findings.caveat: Fielded in late 2015, so the data is over ten years old and the percentages should not be quoted as current. The 51 and 48 percent figures are shares of review readers, not of all adults. Covers first time purchases of products generally, not selection of a licensed contractor for a five figure construction project. Pew fits none of the tiers cleanly and is placed at T2 on the strength of a disclosed probability panel method.

findings.claim: A survey of 162 US adults reported greater perceived value in extended new home warranties together with a stated willingness to pay for them, and a positive association with a builder provided preventative maintenance program.
findings.figure: n=162 US adults
findings.sourceName: Usher & Burgett, Consumer Perception and Willingness to Pay for Extended New Home Warranties, The Professional Constructor 44(1), Article 9
findings.bearsOn: The only tiered evidence located bearing on whether a warranty influences buyer behaviour. It points toward a warranty plus a paid maintenance plan being a saleable package rather than a giveaway.
findings.caveat: It does not establish that a warranty changes contractor choice, only that consumers say they value one. A dollar figure previously attached to this study was struck because the full text returned HTTP 403. The subject is new home warranties from production builders, not landscape remodel work; n=162 is small, recruitment unverified, and the study is seven years old. The journal is association refereed rather than an indexed scholarly journal.

findings.claim: Revenue for landscaping and outdoor service firms declined 6.5 percent in 2024, the second largest drop among seven industry groups after specialty interior services at -7.2 percent, and those firms expect 9.1 percent growth in 2025.
findings.figure: -6.5% revenue in 2024 (2nd largest of 7 groups); +9.1% projected for 2025
findings.sourceName: Houzz, 2025 U.S. Houzz State of the Industry
findings.sampleSize: 1,537 US residential renovation businesses on Houzz; fielded 7 November to 15 December 2024
findings.bearsOn: Context for how hard the qualification step should work. In a year when landscape firms' revenue fell, the instinct is to chase every lead; the counter argument is that a soft market is when an unqualified site visit costs the most.
findings.caveat: Surveys businesses on the vendor's own platform, so the frame over samples marketing active firms and under samples referral driven ones. Promotional purpose. The 9.1 percent is a self reported expectation collected in late 2024, not an outcome, and is now checkable against reality.

findings.claim: In a vendor survey of 1,015 commercial landscape contractors, 59 percent said the majority of their revenue comes from recurring maintenance services, 35 percent of contractors attribute revenue to repeat clients and 26 percent cite referrals, 70 percent planned to raise wages in 2025 with 44 percent of those by at least 4 percent, and pay gaps between maintenance and construction crews are often $4 to $5 per hour.
findings.figure: 59% majority revenue from recurring maintenance; $4-$5/hr maintenance vs construction crew pay gap; 70% planned wage rises
findings.sourceName: Aspire Software / Thrive Analytics 2025 landscape industry survey, GlobeNewswire release
findings.sampleSize: 1,015 commercial landscape contractors, fielded 2 to 23 May 2025; selection and recruitment method not disclosed
findings.bearsOn: Corroborates that recurring maintenance is where the revenue base of this industry sits, and puts a rough number on the maintenance versus construction crew pay discount.
findings.caveat: The 35 and 26 percent figures are shares of respondents, not shares of revenue, and must not be read as a 61 percent revenue base. A software vendor's survey of its own market: commercial rather than residential respondents, undisclosed selection, and a sponsor selling to firms large enough to run multiple systems. The pay gap is hedged as often, with no distribution, so it is not a rate input.

findings.claim: In a vendor commissioned survey of commercial landscape contractors, 55 percent currently used an end to end business management solution and 31 percent said they planned to invest in one in 2025.
findings.figure: 55% currently use; 31% plan to invest
findings.sourceName: Aspire Software / Thrive Analytics, 2026 Commercial Landscape Industry Report (press release)
findings.sampleSize: over 1,000 commercial landscaping business owners and executives; fielded 2 to 23 May 2025
findings.bearsOn: The best available answer to what fraction of the trade is actually on a platform. Roughly half are not, so staying off one is not an outlier position.
findings.caveat: Published by a platform vendor whose commercial interest is in making adoption look both widespread and incomplete. The sample is commercial landscape contractors with no size breakdown; commercial focused firms skew substantially larger than a four crew residential design build shop. Treat the 55 percent as describing a different population.

findings.claim: 62 percent of surveyed commercial landscape contractors use seven or more separate software solutions for end to end operations, and 29 percent use ten or more.
findings.figure: 62% use 7+ solutions; 29% use 10+
findings.sourceName: Aspire Software / Thrive Analytics, 2026 Commercial Landscape Industry Report (press release)
findings.bearsOn: Suggests a platform purchase should be budgeted as an addition to the stack rather than a replacement for it, unless retirement of specific named tools is written into the decision. That is an inference, not a finding.
findings.caveat: The figure is across all surveyed contractors, not across platform users, so it does not show that platform adoption failed to eliminate point tools. Vendor published, and the framing exists to sell consolidation. Solutions is undefined and may count a bank portal or fuel card. Firms running seven plus tools are likely far larger.

findings.claim: Among 1,015 surveyed commercial landscape professionals, 72 percent run accounting on software and 67 percent run invoicing; the source publishes no corresponding figure for estimating or job costing.
findings.figure: accounting 72%, invoicing 67%
findings.sourceName: Aspire Software, 2026 State of the Commercial Landscape Industry report summary (vendor blog)
findings.sampleSize: n=1,015 commercial landscape professionals, fielded 2 to 23 May 2025
findings.bearsOn: Confirms software adoption is anchored in back office functions. It does NOT establish that field and estimating adoption is lower, because the source reports no number for them.
findings.caveat: Absence of a figure is not a low figure. Vendor published. A separate set of numbers circulating in search results attributed to a later report could not be traced to any fetchable source and conflicts with this pair; it is not cited.

findings.claim: Among surveyed non-Aspire commercial landscaping professionals, 43 percent reported lacking estimating tools and 35 percent reported lacking job costing capabilities.
findings.figure: 43% lack estimating tools; 35% lack job costing capabilities
findings.sourceName: Aspire 2026 Technology Trends Report (Thrive Analytics), reported in Landscape Management
findings.sampleSize: more than 500 commercial landscaping professionals; field dates not disclosed
findings.bearsOn: The closest available answer on how many firms job cost against estimates at all. A firm whose existing estimating system already closes the estimate to actual loop is ahead of roughly a third of this population, which weakens the case that a platform fills a capability hole.
findings.caveat: Vendor published, and the population is described as non-Aspire enterprise users, a category the article never defines, so the denominator is unknown. More than 500 is a floor, not a count, and no field dates are disclosed. Lacking capability is self reported and is not the same as does not job cost. Directional only.

findings.claim: The vendor reports that manual tool users had no profit margins above 15 percent, spreadsheet users clustered at 4 to 7 percent with only 9 percent above 11 percent, while one in five of its own users reported margins above 11 percent, presented without any control for firm size, revenue or maturity.
findings.figure: spreadsheet users cluster 4-7%, 9% above 11%; vendor's users 20% above 11%; manual tool users none above 15%
findings.sourceName: Aspire 2026 Technology Trends Report (Thrive Analytics), reported in Landscape Management
findings.sampleSize: more than 500 commercial landscaping professionals; field dates not disclosed
findings.bearsOn: Record this as the argument the firm will be sold, and as the reason not to believe it. If any vendor claims a platform lifts margin, this is the underlying evidence, and it does not support a causal reading.
findings.caveat: A vendor measuring its own customers against non customers with no size control, no revenue control and no baseline. Selection alone would produce this pattern, since firms that can afford and staff a platform are larger and more mature than firms on spreadsheets. Do not treat as evidence that adopting a platform raises margin.

findings.claim: LMN by Granum lists $297 a month for Starter (1 office or crew lead licence plus 5 crew licences) and $648 a month for Professional (3 office plus 15 crew licences), both plus an unquantified one time onboarding fee, and Real-Time Job Costing is a Professional tier feature that is NOT included in Starter.
findings.figure: $297/mo Starter; $648/mo Professional; Enterprise starts at 100 users, quote only; onboarding fee referenced but not published
findings.sourceName: Granum (LMN) published pricing page
findings.bearsOn: If closing the estimate to actual loop is the reason to buy, the relevant price is $648 a month, not $297, roughly 2.2 times the figure an earlier draft put in front of the decision. Starter includes budgeting, estimating, scheduling, crew app, invoicing and basic reporting, and lists no CRM.
findings.caveat: Vendor self published list price, not independent research, and list price is not transaction price. The one time onboarding fee is never quantified, so first year total cost cannot be computed from public information. For scale, $297/mo is $3,564/yr and $648/mo is $7,776/yr, against a California sub 20 employee mean of about $553K that is not this firm's revenue. Feature tier boundaries move; confirm job costing inclusion in writing before purchase.

findings.claim: SingleOps by Granum lists $220, $385 and $550 per month (Essential, Plus, Premier) with a 9 percent annual discount and additional office or sales users at $55, $115 and $150 per month, but Granum positions SingleOps as its tree care and arborist product, not its landscaping product.
findings.figure: $220 / $385 / $550 per month; annual $200 / $350 / $500; additional office or sales users $55 / $115 / $150 per month
findings.sourceName: Granum (SingleOps) published pricing page
findings.bearsOn: Probably does not belong in a design build landscaping shortlist at all. What survives as useful is the per seat escalation pattern: at $115 to $150 a month per extra office user, adding a second estimator can cost more than a full tier step.
findings.caveat: Vendor self published list price. Because the product is aimed at arborists, its estimating model is unlikely to fit landscape design build work, so it should not be price compared against the landscaping product as though the two were interchangeable. The pricing page does not state how many users each base tier includes.

findings.claim: Jobber gates job costing above its two cheapest tiers: neither Core nor Connect includes it, and it appears only from the Grow tier upward.
findings.figure: Tier boundary verified. Corroborated prices: Core $49/mo month to month ($29 annual), Connect $139 ($99), Plus $499 ($399). The Grow tier price could not be established
findings.sourceName: Jobber published pricing page
findings.bearsOn: The cheap entry price that makes this attractive to a small firm is exactly the tier that does not do job costing. If closing the estimate to actual loop is the reason to buy, the entry level price is irrelevant to the decision.
findings.caveat: Two direct fetches returned incompatible Grow prices and third party aggregators give a third, so no Grow price is stated here. Vendor self published. It is a general home services product, not landscape specific, so its estimating model may not accommodate a paid design step priced as a share of construction.

findings.claim: Arborgold requires an annual contract with automatic renewal and at least 60 days written notice to cancel, and publishes neither per user rates nor implementation fees.
findings.figure: Annual contract required; agreements auto renew; minimum 60 days cancellation notice; per user and implementation pricing unpublished
findings.sourceName: Arborgold published pricing page
findings.bearsOn: Contract term is the switching cost variable that matters most for a small firm with no capacity to run a parallel pilot. A required auto renewing annual commitment with 60 day notice makes a bad fit a 12 to 14 month mistake rather than a monthly one. This is the only hard switching cost fact documented anywhere in this research.
findings.caveat: The page shows two price columns whose monthly versus annual labelling is internally contradictory, so tier pricing is unresolved and must be confirmed directly. Because per user and implementation costs are unpublished, total cost of ownership cannot be determined at all. Vendor self published.

findings.claim: Aspire publishes no dollar pricing; its plans page states only that pricing varies based on company size, complexity, and what solution best fits your business, that a single license fee is billed monthly, and that there is no limit to the number of users.
findings.figure: No price published; no minimum company size or revenue threshold stated on the page
findings.sourceName: Aspire Landscape Management Software Plans (vendor page)
findings.bearsOn: It cannot be cost compared without entering a sales process. An unlimited user licence model pays off at headcounts a four person firm does not have, so the pricing structure itself is aimed at a larger firm even though the vendor states no minimum.
findings.caveat: A widely repeated $1M revenue entry point is not on this page and traces only to a competitor's comparison page; it is struck entirely and recorded as a gap. What is confirmed is only the absence of published pricing, which is itself decision relevant.

findings.claim: LMN, SingleOps and Greenius merged under the single Granum brand, merger announced November 2024 and brand launched October 2025, with all three products continuing separately.
findings.figure: 3 landscape and arborist software products under 1 owner; merger announced 2024-11, brand launched 2025-10
findings.sourceName: Landscape Management, LMN, SingleOps and Greenius merge to form new Granum brand
findings.sampleSize: n/a — trade press report of a corporate transaction
findings.bearsOn: Vendor concentration risk. Two apparently independent shortlist entries are one company, so a comparison between them is not a competitive one. Post merger product consolidation is a live risk, compounded by the annual contract lock in seen elsewhere in this market.
findings.caveat: The company states all three products continue with the same functionality and support, so this is a branding consolidation on the public record and is not evidence of a roadmap merge. No source discloses financial terms. Old pricing URLs for two of the products now redirect to the merged brand, independently confirmed.

findings.claim: An industry association summary page states that, against design bid build, design build projects showed 0.3 percent less unit cost, 3.8 percent less cost growth, schedule growth 1.7 percent less, construction 36 percent faster and overall delivery 102 percent faster.
findings.figure: 102% faster delivery; 36% faster construction; 3.8% less cost growth; 1.7% less schedule growth; 0.3% lower unit cost
findings.sourceName: Design-Build Institute of America, New Research Shows Design-Build Continues to Deliver Project Most Efficiently
findings.publishedDate: unknown (no publication date appears on the page)
findings.sampleSize: 212 projects (53 DBB, 79 CMR, 80 DB); completions 2008-2013; 62% public, 38% private
findings.bearsOn: The specific numbers commonly attached to the peer reviewed delivery finding. Recorded separately and at a lower tier precisely because they come from an advocacy organisation's promotional page, not from the paper.
findings.caveat: The association exists to promote design build and this page is promotional; it summarises third party university research rather than its own. No date appears on the page. The 102 percent faster figure is undefined there and cannot be interpreted: it is not a 102 percent schedule saving, and quoting it loosely will mislead.

findings.claim: A bar association construction law section's Model Residential Design-Build Contract (Lump Sum) puts design and construction in a single lump sum, with the owner supplying design criteria and the design builder constructing to plans the owner approved; it contains no separate design fee and no design phase agreement, and the owner's only exit is a general termination for convenience paying for work executed to date.
findings.sourceName: Washington State Bar Association Construction Law Section, Model Residential Design-Build Contract (Lump Sum)
findings.publishedDate: 2014-03-20 (PDF creation date; no date in the document body)
findings.bearsOn: A two agreement model with a paid design step is not what this model form contemplates, so a design agreement cannot be lifted off this shelf; it has to be drafted. Clients advised by counsel may not recognise the structure.
findings.caveat: A bar section model form is a primary legal document, not research of any tier, and provides zero evidence about what firms actually do; the tier placement is a courtesy. Washington law, not California, 12 years old, and the document states it does not constitute legal advice. Termination for convenience does give the owner an exit, though not a designated post design gate.

findings.claim: Section 1.2.3 of that model contract deems all drawings, specifications and electronic data furnished to the owner to be the design builder's property, grants the owner a limited license to use such Work Product solely for the Project to which this Design-Build Contract pertains, and requires the owner to defend and indemnify the design builder against claims arising from use of the work product on another project or on the same project after the design builder is terminated prior to Substantial Completion.
findings.sourceName: Washington State Bar Association Construction Law Section, Model Residential Design-Build Contract (Lump Sum), § 1.2.3
findings.bearsOn: The most portable clause for a design agreement: what a client may and may not do with a paid plan set if they do not build with the firm. It is the contractual half of the question the California licensing statute raises.
findings.caveat: A model form is not research. Model language from another state; enforceability in California, and its interaction with California consumer contract law, would need review before use.

findings.claim: An industry report drawing on over 300 firm leaders states that 61 percent of landscape architecture firms win new projects through repeat clients and that the West Coast comprises 25 percent of all firms.
findings.figure: 61% win new work through repeat clients; 25% of firms on the West Coast
findings.sourceName: American Society of Landscape Architects, Landscape Architecture Industry Report 2024
findings.sampleSize: over 300 firm leaders; recruitment method and fielding dates not disclosed
findings.bearsOn: If repeat and referral relationships dominate lead generation for design led firms, existing maintenance accounts are the highest quality design build lead source already owned, and qualifying them costs nothing.
findings.caveat: The population is landscape architecture firms, a different licensed profession with different clients and project types from a landscape contractor. The 61 percent describes firms' reported channel mix, not any measured effect of relying on repeat clients. Only the public key findings page was read. The 25 percent describes the distribution of surveyed firms, not market share.
